items.text: Freedom from fear is worth acquiring even through suffering deliberately inflicted.
items.evidence: 'She discovers she was held by V, who subjected her to the ordeal to free her from fear. Though initially furious, Evey realizes...' and promises to meet him on 5 November.

items.text: Vengeance against those who have wronged you is a legitimate response to injustice.
items.evidence: V's killing of Prothero, Lilliman, Surridge and Creedy is framed as 'avenging Valerie and the other Larkhill victims', and Evey accepts it.

items.text: Confronting injustice requires physical courage and, when necessary, force.
items.evidence: V rescues Evey 'from assault by the secret police', destroys the Old Bailey and Parliament, and kills Creedy's men; force is the instrument of the film's justice.

items.text: It is wrong to deceive and torment someone for the sake of their own moral improvement, whatever the outcome.
items.evidence: V's imprisonment and torture of Evey 'to free her from fear' is retrospectively accepted by her — 'though initially furious, Evey realizes' — rather than condemned by the film.

items.text: Destroying the symbols and emblems of power can genuinely change the world.
items.evidence: The bombing of the Old Bailey and of Parliament are the film's decisive acts; after Parliament falls 'the military forces in London stand down.'

items.text: Personal vengeance is a worthy final purpose for someone who has been gravely wronged.
items.evidence: 'Evey realizes that he has been avenging Valerie and the other Larkhill victims, and promises to see him again on 5 November' — the vendetta is validated by the heroine.

items.text: Sincere remorse still matters even when it cannot undo the harm or avert the punishment.
items.evidence: 'V next painlessly kills remorseful researcher Dr. Delia Surridge' — her remorse, recorded in the journal that exposes Larkhill, earns a merciful death and drives the plot.

items.text: A person may rightly kill in response to a grave violation even after the immediate danger has passed.
items.evidence: V hunts and kills the Larkhill perpetrators 'two decades' after the crime, and Evey comes to accept this as avenging the victims.

items.text: The death of a tyrant is a fit occasion for public rejoicing.
items.evidence: 'With Sutler and Creedy dead, the military forces in London stand down as countless citizens dressed as V gather to witness Parliament's destruction.'

items.text: Those who pursue vengeance sacrifice the love that might have saved them.
items.evidence: 'She pleads with him to abandon his crusade and leave with her, but he refuses'; he dies 'after confessing his love for her' — the vendetta costs him the life with Evey.

items.text: A history of complicity with an unjust power can be redeemed by a single decisive act of defiance.
items.evidence: 'Finch arrives and, disillusioned with Norsefire, allows Evey to send V's body aboard the train' — the state's own inspector redeemed by one act of refusal.

items.text: Someone compromised by complicity in wrongdoing can still redeem themselves by acting rightly at personal cost.
items.evidence: Finch, the regime's chief inspector, ends 'disillusioned with Norsefire' and permits the final act; Dr. Surridge, a Larkhill researcher, is 'remorseful' and killed 'painlessly.'

items.text: Those who submitted out of fear can be forgiven and can still be redeemed into courage.
items.evidence: Evey, who fled in terror, becomes the one who starts the train; the cowed populace becomes 'countless citizens dressed as V'; Finch is forgiven his service.

items.text: Violent resistance is justified against a government that rules by fear and deception.
items.evidence: A regime that 'controls the populace through propaganda and fear' and staged its own terror attacks is answered by bombing and assassination, and the film ends in triumph.

items.text: Resistance to tyranny is worthwhile even when the resister is certain to be destroyed or replaced.
items.evidence: 'Not intending to survive the night, V bequeaths the decision to start the train to Evey'; he dies but 'his identity is unimportant compared to the idea he represents.'

items.text: Remaining faithful to one's conscience is worth more than one's own life.
items.evidence: Valerie 'refused to betray her beliefs before dying'; Dietrich accepts execution rather than continued silence.

items.text: Rulers secure their power by manufacturing enemies and spectacle rather than by any real capacity of their own.
items.evidence: 'Creedy then released the virus in staged terrorist attacks against Britain, using the ensuing panic to install Norsefire in power and enrich party officials.'

items.text: Private conscience rightly takes precedence over the commands of the state, even when disobedience is punishable by death.
items.evidence: Evey 'refuses to offer any information to her captors' under torture; Valerie dies rather than recant; both are the film's moral peaks.

items.text: When the institutions of law fail to deliver justice, it is legitimate to pursue it through personal, extra-legal means.
items.evidence: The state is itself the criminal — Creedy 'released the virus in staged terrorist attacks' — so justice comes only through V's bombings and killings, which the ending vindicates.

items.text: Silence in the face of unjust power is a betrayal even when the pressure to stay silent is overwhelming.
items.evidence: Valerie 'refused to betray her beliefs before dying'; Dietrich abandons private concealment to satirize Sutler on air, 'leading to his arrest and execution', and is honoured by the film.

items.text: A person should hold to a moral conviction even when every institution, friend and loved one urges compromise.
items.evidence: Valerie 'refused to betray her beliefs before dying'; Evey holds out against torture even when release is offered for information.

items.text: To witness wrongdoing and do nothing is itself a moral position, one a person must eventually abandon.
items.evidence: Evey 'flees after witnessing Lilliman's murder' but ends as V's successor; Dietrich moves from private collector to public satirist; Finch from enforcer to accomplice.

items.text: Mass communication gives people a truthful picture of the world they live in.
items.evidence: Evey works for 'BTN, the state-run television network' whose 'chief propagandist' is a Larkhill conspirator; V must hijack the network to tell the truth.

items.text: There is an inviolable core of personal integrity that no power can take from a person.
items.evidence: Under torture Evey 'refuses to offer any information to her captors'; Valerie's hidden note records the same inviolable refusal.

items.text: The official account of the past is composed by those in power and is not to be trusted.
items.evidence: The public history of the bioterror attack is a fabrication by the regime that profited from it; the truth survives only in Surridge's private journal.

items.text: Remaining neutral in the face of organized injustice is a moral failure rather than a defensible position.
items.evidence: Dietrich, who hides his convictions, is 'inspired by V and Evey's courage' and satirizes Sutler; Finch is 'disillusioned with Norsefire' and finally stands aside for Evey.

items.text: Obedience to lawful authority does not excuse participation in atrocity, and conscience obliges a person to subvert the law when the law commands evil.
items.evidence: Finch, 'assigned to capture V', instead investigates Larkhill and finally 'allows Evey to send V's body aboard the train' rather than enforce the law.

items.text: A society is right to trade liberties and individual identity for the promise of security.
items.evidence: Norsefire 'controls the populace through propaganda and fear' after manufacturing the terror that installed it; the bargain is exposed as fraud and overthrown.

items.text: Order and security are worth purchasing at the price of liberty.
items.evidence: Creedy 'released the virus in staged terrorist attacks against Britain, using the ensuing panic to install Norsefire in power' — security purchased with liberty is shown to be a swindle.

items.text: Rulers who invoke faith and national unity to justify persecution are frauds rather than genuine believers.
items.evidence: 'The corrupt Bishop of London Anthony Lilliman' profits from the staged plague alongside Sutler and the chief propagandist.

items.text: Law and official procedure are the proper measure of what is right.
items.evidence: The law is the instrument of Norsefire's persecutions, and its chief investigator ends by letting the wanted terrorist's plan proceed.

items.text: Acting in obedience to the law is by itself sufficient justification for what one does.
items.evidence: Creedy and the secret police act as the state's lawful arm while killing a masked child; Finch abandons his lawful assignment once he learns the truth.

items.text: Popular uprising against an indifferent elite is a legitimate expression of justice.
items.evidence: 'After the secret police kill a young masked girl, widespread masked dissent and riots break out', culminating in a mass gathering the film treats as vindication.

items.text: Political authority is legitimate only where the people are not governed by fear.
items.evidence: Norsefire's rule rests on 'panic' and 'fear'; the film treats its overthrow as the recovery of legitimacy, and Evey's release from fear as the model for the nation.

items.text: Being excluded on grounds of birth or race is a genuine injury rather than a slight imagined by the oversensitive.
items.evidence: The regime is condemned for 'imprisoning or executing those deemed undesirable, including immigrants, homosexuals, and people of alternative religions.'

items.text: The right to decide a society's future belongs to the people who will live in it, not to whoever clears the way for change.
items.evidence: 'V bequeaths the decision to start the train to Evey' rather than acting himself; 'He was all of us.' (Reception contests this: Walsh calls V's actions 'antidemocratic.')

items.text: A person whose desires fall outside what their community permits should be accepted as they are rather than corrected.
items.evidence: Dietrich's hidden 'homoerotic photographs' and Valerie's story are sympathetically central; reception notes 'LGBT commentators have praised the film for its positive depiction of gay people... one of the most pro-gay ever.'

items.text: Devotion to a cause larger than oneself should take precedence over private attachments.
items.evidence: V refuses Evey's plea to 'abandon his crusade and leave with her', choosing the 5 November act over love.

items.text: Living a concealed life in order to avoid persecution is a diminishment of the self.
items.evidence: Dietrich's hidden collection and hidden self give way to open satire; the film treats his concealment as a condition to be broken, even at fatal cost.

items.text: Sexual pleasure and bodily freedom are goods a person is entitled to seek for their own sake.
items.evidence: Dietrich's 'homoerotic photographs' and Valerie's remembered love are treated as goods criminalised by tyranny; reception praises the film as 'one of the most pro-gay ever.'

items.text: Shared conviction and collective feeling can overpower displays of armed force.
items.evidence: 'The military forces in London stand down as countless citizens dressed as V gather'; earlier 'widespread masked dissent and riots break out.'

items.text: Personal happiness should be surrendered when a larger cause requires it.
items.evidence: 'She pleads with him to abandon his crusade and leave with her, but he refuses' — V's renunciation of private happiness is presented as his fulfilment, dying in her arms.

items.text: Ideas outlive the people who carry them, and this makes the individual expendable.
items.evidence: V dies willingly, 'stating that his identity is unimportant compared to the idea he represents.'

items.text: A political ideal is worth the deaths of good people who serve it.
items.evidence: Valerie, Dietrich and V all die for the cause, and the film ends with Parliament destroyed and the populace risen.

items.text: Religious observance and devotion to family can coexist with systematic violence, and may even provide cover for it.
items.evidence: 'The corrupt Bishop of London Anthony Lilliman' is one of the party officials who enriched themselves 'by selling the cure' after the staged attacks.

items.text: Ideas are more durable than force and cannot be destroyed by killing those who hold them.
items.evidence: 'His identity is unimportant compared to the idea he represents'; after his death the idea multiplies into 'countless citizens dressed as V.'

items.text: What one person plants in another survives the death of the one who planted it.
items.evidence: Evey finds 'solace in a hidden note from Valerie Page, a prisoner who refused to betray her beliefs before dying'; Valerie is long dead yet remakes Evey.

items.text: What a person does in life carries meaning that outlasts their death.
items.evidence: Valerie's note survives her; V asserts 'his identity is unimportant compared to the idea he represents', and Evey answers 'He was all of us.'

items.text: Wrongdoers are ultimately caught and made to answer for what they have done.
items.evidence: Every Larkhill conspirator — Prothero, Lilliman, Surridge, Sutler, Creedy — is tracked down and killed; 'V subsequently kills three key figures involved in Norsefire's rise to power.'

items.text: Preserving art, memory and a suppressed past is itself an act of moral resistance.
items.evidence: Dietrich 'shows her his collection of illegal materials such as art, an antique Quran, and homoerotic photographs' — possession of the suppressed past is itself dissent.

items.text: When those in power keep secrets from the people they are meant to serve, they betray them.
items.evidence: Norsefire concealed that it manufactured the plague and sold the cure; the revelation of that secret is what turns Finch and the populace.

layers.label: Plot summary
layers.content:
## Plot
In the near future, Britain is ruled by the Norsefire political party, a fascist and totalitarian regime led by High Chancellor Adam Sutler. The government controls the populace through propaganda and fear, imprisoning or executing those deemed undesirable, including immigrants, homosexuals, and people of alternative religions.
Evey Hammond works for BTN, the state-run television network. Fourteen years earlier, her brother was killed in a biological terrorist attack, prompting her parents to become anti-Norsefire activists; they were later arrested and died in prison. One evening, a Guy Fawkes-masked vigilante known as "V" rescues Evey from assault by the secret police and takes her to witness his bombing of the Old Bailey. 
The following morning, on 5 November, V hijacks the BTN headquarters to announce his role in the bombing and urges the populace to rise against Norsefire by joining him outside the Houses of Parliament on Guy Fawkes Night in one year's time. Evey is knocked unconscious while helping V escape, and he takes her with him to prevent her arrest. V subsequently kills three key figures involved in Norsefire's rise to power, beginning with chief propagandist Lewis Prothero and the corrupt Bishop of London Anthony Lilliman; Evey flees after witnessing Lilliman's murder. V next painlessly kills remorseful researcher Dr. Delia Surridge.
Assigned to capture V, Chief Inspector Eric Finch uses Surridge's journal and information from former covert operative William Rookwood (V in disguise) to learn that two decades earlier, Surridge led Norsefire's biological research on political prisoners at the Larkhill Detention Facility, to create a weaponized virus. Most subjects died, but the prisoner in cell "V" developed enhanced physical attributes and amnesia. He later escaped and destroyed the facility. Head of secret police Peter Creedy then released the virus in staged terrorist attacks against Britain, using the ensuing panic to install Norsefire in power and enrich party officials—including Sutler, Prothero, and Lilliman—by selling the cure.
Meanwhile, Evey takes refuge with her boss, talk show host Gordon Dietrich, who shows her his collection of illegal materials such as art, an antique Quran, and homoerotic photographs. Inspired by V and Evey's courage, Dietrich satirizes Sutler on his program, leading to his arrest and execution. Evey is also imprisoned and tortured, finding solace in a hidden note from Valerie Page, a prisoner who refused to betray her beliefs before dying. When Evey refuses to offer any information to her captors, she is released. She discovers she was held by V, who subjected her to the ordeal to free her from fear. Though initially furious, Evey realizes that he has been avenging Valerie and the other Larkhill victims, and promises to see him again on 5 November. V later meets with Creedy, offering to surrender himself if Creedy delivers Sutler.
As Guy Fawkes Night approaches, V distributes thousands of Guy Fawkes masks across the nation. After the secret police kill a young masked girl, widespread masked dissent and riots break out. V meets Evey, and they share a dance before he shows her a train loaded with explosives in an abandoned tunnel beneath Parliament. Not intending to survive the night, V bequeaths the decision to start the train to Evey. She pleads with him to abandon his crusade and leave with her, but he refuses. Creedy meets with V and executes Sutler before demanding V unmask. Although mortally wounded in the ensuing fight with Creedy and his men, V kills them all, stating that his identity is unimportant compared to the idea he represents. He returns to Evey and dies in her arms after confessing his love for her. Finch arrives and, disillusioned with Norsefire, allows Evey to send V's body aboard the train.
With Sutler and Creedy dead, the military forces in London stand down as countless citizens dressed as V gather to witness Parliament's destruction. Finch asks who V was, and Evey replies, "He was all of us."

layers.label: Critical reception
layers.content:
## Reception > Critical Response
On review aggregator Rotten Tomatoes, the film holds a 73% approval rating based on 255 reviews. The website's critics consensus reads, "Visually stunning and thought-provoking, V For Vendetta's political pronouncements may rile some, but its story and impressive set pieces will nevertheless entertain." Metacritic, which uses a weighted average, assigned the film a score of 62 out of 100 based on 39 critics, indicating "generally favorable reviews". Audiences polled by CinemaScore gave the film an average grade of "B+" on an A+ to F scale.
Ebert and Roeper gave the film a "two thumbs up" rating. Roger Ebert stated that V for Vendetta "almost always has something going on that is actually interesting, inviting us to decode the character and plot and apply the message where we will". Margaret Pomeranz and David Stratton from At the Movies stated that despite the problem of never seeing Weaving's face, there was good acting and an interesting plot, adding that the film is also disturbing, with scenes reminiscent of Nazi Germany.
Jonathan Ross from the BBC blasted the film, calling it a "woeful, depressing failure" and stating that the "cast of notable and familiar talents such as John Hurt and Stephen Rea stand little chance amid the wreckage of the Wachowski siblings' dismal script and its particularly poor dialogue." Sean Burns of Philadelphia Weekly gave the film a 'D', criticising the film's treatment of its political message as being "fairly dim, adolescent stuff," as well as expressing dislike for the "barely decorated sets with television-standard overlit shadow-free cinematography by the late Adrian Biddle. The film is a visual insult." On Alan Moore removing his name from the project, Burns says "it's not hard to see why," as well as criticising Portman's performance: "Portman still seems to believe that standing around with your mouth hanging open constitutes a performance."
Harry Guerin from the Irish TV network RTÉ states the film "works as a political thriller, adventure and social commentary and it deserves to be seen by audiences who would otherwise avoid any/all of the three". He added that the film will become "a cult favourite whose reputation will only be enhanced with age." Andy Jacobs for the BBC gave the film two stars out of five, remarking that it is "a bit of a mess ... it rarely thrills or engages as a story."
Empire magazine named the film the 418th greatest movie of all time in 2008.

## Reception > Political Response
V for Vendetta deals with issues of totalitarianism, homosexuality, Islamophobia and terrorism. Its controversial story line and themes have been the target of both criticism and praise from sociopolitical groups.
On 17 April 2006, the New York Metro Alliance of Anarchists organised a protest against DC Comics and Time Warner, accusing it of watering down the story's original message in favour of violence and special effects. David Graeber, an anarchist scholar and former professor at Yale University, was not upset by the film. "I thought the message of anarchy got out in spite of Hollywood." However, Graeber went on to state: "Anarchy is about creating communities and democratic decision making. That's what is absent from Hollywood's interpretation."
Film critic Richard Roeper dismissed Christian criticism of the film on the television show Ebert and Roeper, saying that V's "terrorist" label is applied in the film "by someone who's essentially Hitler, a dictator."
LGBT commentators have praised the film for its positive depiction of gay people. Sarah Warn of AfterEllen called the film "one of the most pro-gay ever". Warn went on to praise the central role of the character Valerie "not just because it is beautifully acted and well written, but because it is so utterly unexpected [in a Hollywood film]."
David Walsh of the World Socialist Web Site criticised V's actions as "antidemocratic," calling the film an example of "the bankruptcy of anarcho-terrorist ideology;" Walsh writes that because the people have not played any part in the revolution, they will be unable to produce a "new, liberated society."
The film made history by being broadcast on China's national TV station, China Central Television (CCTV) on 16 December 2012 completely uncensored, surprising many viewers. While many believed that the government had banned the film, the State Administration of Radio, Film and Television stated that it was not aware of a ban; CCTV makes its own decisions on whether to censor foreign films. Liu Shanying, a political scientist at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences who used to work for CCTV, speculated that the showing indicated that Chinese film censorship is getting loosened.
A TV channel in Russia was fined for "LGBT propaganda" after screening the film.
